abstract: LLMs can repair noisy OCR transcripts of historical documents, but they also change text that was already correct. We propose EditVeto, a veto gate placed after a full-context LLM rewrite. The rewrite is character-aligned to the OCR input, its differences are split into blocks, and a 0.6B-parameter gate keeps or reverts each block. An oracle analysis motivates the design: given the true error locations, per-span generation is worse than no correction, whereas vetoing a full rewrite’s edits helps. Trained on rewrites by two Qwen3 models and evaluated, frozen, on the eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, the gate improves all five rewriters tested, two of them unseen in training: weighted cMER falls by 0.0026–0.0044 and the preference score rises by 0.15–0.25 (paired bootstrap, $p\approx 0.0002$ each). On published competition outputs it lowers cMER for three of four teams but raises it for the winning run (0.0050 to 0.0065). In a second, disclosed test look, a retrained gate still improves LoRA-tuned rewriters (cMER $-0.0011$ to $-0.0021$), and an ensemble of their gated edits reaches a cMER of 0.0069 and a preference score of 0.928, mostly through fine-tuning and pooling rather than gating. Built only on public models and data, it is behind the winner (0.0050) and tied with the second-ranked run (0.0071), both from the only team using domain pre-training, and ahead of all other published runs. A third, secondary look shows the unchanged gate improving zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B (cMER 0.0114 to 0.0108) but only the preference score of its LoRA-tuned version.

sections.body: The paper observes that LLM post-correction of OCR text also edits text that was already correct. On the development set, with oracle error spans, per-span generation by Qwen3-8B scores cMER 0.0562 against 0.0275 for no correction. Vetoing the edits of a full-context rewrite instead improves both metrics. EditVeto applies this idea: a rewrite is aligned to the OCR input, split into edit blocks, and each block is kept or reverted by a learned gate. The gate is trained on blocks from two Qwen3 rewriters and then tested frozen. The text also reports a disclosed second test look with retrained gates and LoRA-tuned rewriters, a secondary third look, and states that the gate does not help every system.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: LLM rewrites of OCR transcripts also change correct text, so the paper proposes a learned gate that vetoes collateral edits.

sections.body: The section places the work among post-OCR correction methods. Earlier systems used noisy-channel models and neural sequence-to-sequence translation. Recent work applies LLMs zero-shot or after fine-tuning, and one evaluation concluded that LLMs were not yet effective at the task. Constrained methods, including copy mechanisms, lexically constrained decoding, and decoder-side interpolation for OCR correction, shape generation itself. The authors' gate instead acts after correction, on edits a rewriter has proposed. It leaves decoding unchanged and needs only the input and output text.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier post-OCR methods generate corrections directly, whereas this work filters a finished LLM rewrite at the level of edit blocks.

sections.body: The section defines the input, the official normalization, and the metrics. cMER is (S+D+I)/(H+S+D+I), summed over a test set before the ratio. The preference score counts improved units as +1, unchanged as 0, and degraded as -1. A rewriter's full corrected unit is split into edit blocks, and a gate chooses which blocks to accept; vetoed blocks restore the OCR text. Proposition 1 states that with no accepted blocks the output equals the OCR input, that accepted and vetoed edits split the raw edit distance, and that the normalized error count is bounded by the smaller of two terms. The authors checked the raw-string claims on 4,488 logged outputs. The normalized analogue of the split fails for 1,375 of 98,736 block subsets.
sections.heading: Problem Definition
sections.headline: The task is scored by normalized cMER and a preference score, and a veto keeps a subset of rewrite edits with a bounded error.

sections.body: EditVeto has three parts: a rewriter, an alignment step, and a gate. The rewriter sees the whole unit. The alignment uses a Levenshtein edit script from rapidfuzz, merging adjacent non-matching operations into blocks. The gate uses a Qwen3-0.6B backbone with last-token pooling, concatenated with 15 standardized numeric features and an MLP head with one hidden layer of 256 units. Six features are token log-probability statistics, which the text-only variant sets to zero. Training uses blocks from zero-shot Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B rewrites of the training split, labeled by whether they reduce cMER. One global threshold was chosen on held-out training blocks: 0.5065 for the full gate and 0.4990 for the text-only gate. Held-out ROC-AUC was 0.952 and 0.949.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A full-context rewrite is split into character edit blocks, and a 0.6B-parameter gate keeps or reverts each block.

sections.body: The section sets out data, metrics, and protocol. The HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets form eight cells: three dta19 noise levels, icdar2017 English and French, and three impresso-snippets languages. The official scorer drops units flagged `exclude_from_icdar_evaluation`, leaving 590 scored units. Overall numbers are weighted means in which each dta19 level has weight 1/3. Development uses 518 units in seven cells plus 30 overproof units. Significance comes from a paired bootstrap with 10,000 resamples. Rewriters are Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, which train the gate; Mistral-Small-24B and Qwen2.5-72B, unseen in training; and a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B. Look 1 was frozen and run once. Baselines are the published competition runs.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Evaluation uses eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, the official scorer, paired bootstrap tests, and three separately reported test looks.

sections.body: The section uses reference-based oracle gates on the development set, which are not valid systems. Given exact error spans, Qwen3-8B generating one replacement per span scores cMER 0.0562 with preference -0.6247, against 0.0275 and 0 for no correction. Of 13,167 oracle spans, 5,229 proposals were rejected and 4,677 echoed the OCR span. A window interface still scores 0.0255 with preference 0.2627, below the unfiltered rewrite. Applying the oracle span gate to the full zero-shot rewrite lowers cMER from 0.0247 to 0.0229 and raises preference from 0.4161 to 0.6501. The reverse span gate is worse than no correction, so the gain comes from which blocks are kept. Block granularity beats character granularity.
sections.heading: Motivation: Oracle Analysis (Development Set)
sections.headline: With oracle error spans, per-span generation is worse than no correction, while vetoing edits of a full rewrite lowers cMER from 0.0247 to 0.0229.

sections.body: Development results for the frozen gates on all five rewriters. The full gate lowers weighted cMER by 13% for Qwen3-8B, 27% for Qwen3-32B, 19% for LoRA, 47% for Mistral-Small-24B, and 38% for Qwen2.5-72B. Each difference is significant on both metrics, with p≤0.0008, and cMER changes range from -0.0032 for Qwen3-8B to -0.0118 for Mistral-Small-24B. The gate closes 68%, 70%, 50%, 84%, and 74% of the cMER gap to the label oracle, which reads the reference. A gate trained on one Qwen3 rewriter loses at most 0.0004 cMER on the other. Removing log-probability features changes cMER by -0.0002 to +0.0004 on the Qwen3 rewriters. On the two unseen rewriters, the text-only gate stays within 0.0005 cMER but is lower on preference by 0.02–0.06.
sections.heading: Learned Gate: Development Results
sections.headline: On development data, the frozen gate lowers weighted cMER for all five rewriters, including two never seen in training.

sections.body: Test results from look 1, the first frozen run. The full gate lowers weighted cMER for all five rewriters by 0.0026–0.0044 and raises preference from 0.49–0.71 to 0.71–0.85, with every difference significant at the bootstrap resolution. The text-only gate matches the full gate in cMER to four decimals for four rewriters. The best look-1 system is Qwen2.5-72B with the full gate, at 0.0106 and 0.8446. On icdar2017-fr the gate raises cMER for four of five rewriters, by 0.0012–0.0023. On published competition outputs, the text-only gate lowers cMER for BLOCR, both L3i runs, and Zakaria-ENSIAS. It raises cMER for BnF-Mistral run 1 from 0.0050 to 0.0065 and for run 3 from 0.0071 to 0.0077, while raising preference for every run.
sections.heading: Test Results
sections.headline: On test, the frozen gate lowers cMER for all five rewriters by 0.0026–0.0044, but raises it for the winning competition run.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the claims. The gate is useful for vetoing collateral edits of a full-context rewrite, not for driving generation span by span. Trained on Qwen3 blocks, the frozen gate improves all five rewriters on both metrics, including two unseen in training, and also in a text-only variant. In the second look, a retrained gate still improves LoRA-tuned rewriters, by less than zero-shot ones. The ensemble reaches cMER 0.0069, tied with the second-ranked competition run and behind the winner at 0.0050. The text says most of that gain comes from fine-tuning and pooling. In the third look, the same gate improves a newer zero-shot rewriter but only the preference score of its LoRA version. The authors describe the gate as a safeguard and as complementary to domain pre-training.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The gate helps the tested rewriters, and a pooled fine-tuned ensemble reaches 0.0069 cMER, behind the winner's 0.0050.

sections.body: The appendix gives the proof of Proposition 1 and its checks. The checks cover 4,488 logged development and probe outputs and 98,736 block subsets, where the normalized analogue of the split fails for 1,375 subsets. It then lists development tables for the oracle analysis, per-cell results, and the full gate on five rewriters. Test tables give the frozen and text-only gates, per-cell cMER, and bootstrap differences for the competition runs. The third-look section gives the candidate pools, the ensemble C design, its development and test results, and its protocol. It ends with GPU-hour totals for each phase of the project.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix holds the Proposition 1 proof and checks, development and test tables, third-look design, and compute usage.
